title: AI in Education #12: Five Things I Learned from Zach Groshell about What's Actually Inside the Alpha School Maths Apps
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the twelfth installment of his AI in Education interview series, Craig Barton talks with Zach Groshell, a former fourth-grade teacher and now the first learning scientist on the team building Alpha School's maths apps, about what is actually inside those apps. Groshell's central claim is that AI only returns what the user's own knowledge lets them put in: he builds lessons by working through Engelmann's Direct Instruction programs by hand first, then hands only the mechanical assembly to AI, because early attempts to let technologists (rather than domain experts) generate lessons directly failed immediately. The Alpha maths app itself is not a chatbot but a near-silent, tightly atomised screen experience built on Engelmann's capital-DI principles — short exposures, heavy review (roughly 90% of any lesson), and carefully sequenced examples and non-examples rather than long explanations. Groshell also argues that good retrieval practice should retire itself: once a sub-skill is reliably subsumed into a larger routine, retesting it in isolation wastes time, and retrieval should shift to the composite routine instead. The piece closes on a twist Barton clearly finds instructive: Groshell, who builds the Alpha apps, chose a different model (Montessorium) for his own daughter, illustrating his broader point that the apps are an efficient two-hour engine for foundational skills, not a substitute for the rest of a child's education.
points: AI is only as good as the domain knowledge the user brings to it: Groshell builds lessons by working through Engelmann's Direct Instruction material by hand first and only hands the mechanical assembly to AI, because Alpha's early attempt to let non-experts generate lessons directly failed outright.

The Alpha maths app is built on Engelmann's Direct Instruction, not a conversational AI tutor — a largely silent screen with tiny steps, parallel strands, and roughly 90% review content, designed and field-tested by humans and merely delivered by the machine.

Groshell's 'just tell them' philosophy actually means carefully sequenced examples and non-examples rather than long explanations — a bad teaching sequence explains at length then dumps practice on the child, while good Direct Instruction rules out wrong interpretations through tight example sequences.

Retrieval practice should retire itself: once a sub-skill (e.g. identifying digits in column addition) is reliably subsumed into a larger routine, re-testing it in isolation wastes time — retrieval should shift to the composite routine at increasing levels of sophistication.

Despite building the Alpha apps himself, Groshell chose a different school model (Montessorium, with human-led afternoons) for his own daughter — illustrating his view that the apps are an efficient engine for foundational skills in the morning, not a replacement for the rest of a child's schooling.
quotes: Zach could ask Claude to teach adding 4 + 3, take what it gives, ask for it “a different way”, and deploy the result. Instead, he does the opposite. He digs into the actual Engelmann programs, reads, copies and edits the material by hand, and only once he has it right in his head does he hand the assembly to the AI.

The early assumption was that the technology people could generate the lessons themselves - they had the tools, they could make it slick and bug-free. It failed straight away. You need the domain experts in the loop. Engelmann knew this decades ago, which is why he paired his instructional-design brain with subject-matter experts in history, science and maths.

The child rarely watches for more than about 9 seconds before they have to respond. The steps are tiny. Several strands run in parallel and get chained together, typically across three exposures over three days, before a timed mastery test. Roughly 90% of any lesson is review; only about 10% is the new, slightly harder thing. As Zach put it, it is cognitive load theory in a bottle.

A lot of retrieval, Zach argues - especially in maths - is what he bluntly calls dumb retrieval. We pick a small skill, decide it is “a thing”, and dutifully space it out across the whole year on an ever-expanding interval. But if a child is now doing column addition, identifying the digits and setting out the problem, is already baked into the task.

Zach chose Montessorium for his daughter. Not because he doubts the apps - he builds them - but because she loves reading whole books, journaling and drawing, and the sport-in-the-afternoon model would do nothing for her. The apps, in other words, are not a school.
